stances.claim: Last March 23 2026, CJP wrote about three super ladies -- Cecile Licad, Lea Salonga, and Lisa Macuja-Elizalde -- whose talents have carried the Philippine flag onto the global performing-arts stage. Despite their achievements, none of them had been formally recognized as a 'National Artist (NA).' Today, CJP looks into the NA-conferment law and jurisprudence.

The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) -- created by RA 7356 on April 3 1992 -- administers the conferment. Together with the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP), NCCA was granted by that law the sole prerogative to recommend to the President the 'Order of National Artists' for Filipino citizens who have contributed to building a Filipino sense of nationhood through their art forms. In Almario v. Executive Secretary (July 16 2013), the SC held that the President's discretion is limited to names submitted by NCCA and CCP -- the President cannot confer the Order on anyone not in the final list of NA nominees.

CJP will no longer inquire nor belabor his 'wonderment' why -- despite Cecile's universal excellence in music, Lea's triumphs on the world's most prestigious stages, and Lisa's influence through ballet worldwide -- these ladies have not landed in the final list. Without begrudging the NAs or belittling their achievements (and indeed lauding them), CJP believes Cecile, Lea, and Lisa merit a separate category recognizing distinction that transcends national recognition. Their achievements acquire doctrinal relevance -- each has long been part of NA discussions.
stances.rhetorical_move: no-more-belabor-wonderment + transcends-national-recognition framing without begrudging NAs

stances.claim: What becomes evident is the presence of an institutional gap where recognition for globally-distinguished Filipino artists ought to stand. The President can fill this gap by creating the 'Order of Global Filipino Artists' or GFA via the issuance of an executive order specifically for artists of Philippine ancestry (one or both parents Filipino at the awardee's birth) and giving the same, if not better, privileges and honors as the NAs. In time, Congress may institutionalize this category by granting congressional recognition.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-gap diagnosis + GFA-executive-order-creation + Filipino-ancestry-eligibility + congressional-institutionalization sequence

stances.claim: Marcos Sr. initiated the NA Award via Proclamation No. 1001 (April 27 1972), refined by Proclamation No. 1144 (May 15 1973) and Presidential Decree No. 208 (June 7 1973). He likewise issued Proclamation No. 1151 (June 7 1973) -- the 'Award and Decoration for International Artists' intended for FOREIGN talents whose works have contributed to Philippine arts and culture, premised on 'the arts and letters are universal media of expression free of the confines of geography and nationality.' Those honored were granted privileges similar to NAs during their stay in the Philippines. In 1976/1977, pianist Van Cliburn (USA), prima ballerina Margot Fonteyn (UK), and ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev (USSR/France) were the first to be proclaimed; in 1982, renowned Russian cellist/conductor Mstislav Rostropovich was recognized following his CCP performance.

In this light, the notion of an 'International Artist' must be reimagined. The current executive issuances and statutory framework do not fully recognize Filipino artists who belong to a distinct class -- the Filipino diaspora -- whose contributions to Philippine arts and culture are acclaimed not only within our shores but across the globe: the Global Filipino Artists. After the GFA honor is created by executive fiat and the super ladies selected as the first GFAs, CJP believes the conferment should be held at Malacañan Palace, the CCP, or PICC -- 'the very institutions that have long stood as the sanctuaries of our artistic heritage.' More than ceremonial recognition, the President may fittingly invite the three GFAs to perform and transform the conferment into a living testament to Filipino excellence before both the nation and the world.
stances.rhetorical_move: reimagine-International-Artist + Filipino-diaspora distinct-class + venue-and-performance conferment-format proposal

stances.claim: The question is no longer whether they are worthy -- they have long proven that they are. The more compelling inquiry is whether our institutional frameworks can welcome a new dimension of artistic excellence that is global in reach, yet unmistakably, indelibly Filipino in essence.

notable_anecdotes: The companion-column structural design -- E10 (March 23) raised the wonderment, E09 (April 20) provides the legal framework + policy proposal -- demonstrating CJP's two-column complaint-to-proposal arc as advocacy strategy.

The Almario v. Executive Secretary (July 16 2013) citation -- the doctrinal anchor that explains why CJP cannot simply call on the President to confer NA on Cecile/Lea/Lisa: the President is institutionally locked-in to the NCCA-CCP-submitted list.

The 'I will no longer inquire, nor will I belabor my wonderment why ... these ladies have not landed in the final list' framing -- CJP's diplomatic refusal to speculate on NCCA-CCP internal selection criteria, redirecting energy from NCCA-criticism toward presidential-executive-creativity proposal.

The Marcos-Sr-Proclamation-No.-1001 + Proclamation-No.-1144 + PD No. 208 + Proclamation-No. 1151 catalog -- a tight historical legal-instrument enumeration demonstrating that the President historically has had broad executive-fiat power to establish state-arts-honors.

The International Artist precedents -- Van Cliburn (1976/77 USA pianist) + Margot Fonteyn (UK prima ballerina) + Rudolf Nureyev (USSR/France ballet) + Mstislav Rostropovich (1982 Russian cellist/conductor) -- a cross-Cold-War-Iron-Curtain quartet of world-class performers proclaimed by Marcos Sr., providing both historical-precedent and rhetorical-elevation for the GFA proposal.

The 'arts and letters are universal media of expression free of the confines of geography and nationality' Marcos-Sr verbatim citation -- captured as foundational philosophical-premise that GFA proposal extends in a new direction.
The conferment-venue trinity -- Malacañan Palace + CCP + PICC -- 'sanctuaries of our artistic heritage' -- among CJP's most architecturally-rooted state-honor venue catalogs.

The 'invite the three GFAs to perform and transform the conferment into a living testament' detail -- CJP's innovative performance-as-conferment-format suggestion that would distinguish GFA ceremony from typical static-honor pinning.

The 'global in reach, yet unmistakably, indelibly Filipino in essence' closing -- among CJP's tightest Filipino-diaspora-identity formulations, capturing the both/and that GFA category is meant to honor.

The Filipino-ancestry definition -- 'one or both parents were Filipinos at the birth of the awardee' -- CJP's pragmatic biological-citizenship eligibility test, broadly accommodating mixed-heritage diaspora artists.

The two-tier institutionalization plan -- President-creates-via-EO-first, Congress-may-institutionalize-later -- captures CJP's understanding of executive-precedence-followed-by-legislative-permanence sequence for state-honor establishment.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the companion-column to his March 23 2026 'Why not Cecile, Lea, and Lisa,' pivoting from the wonderment-complaint about three super ladies (Cecile Licad, Lea Salonga, Lisa Macuja-Elizalde) not being recognized as National Artists toward a legal-framework survey and a concrete policy proposal. The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) -- created by RA 7356 on April 3 1992 -- administers the NA conferment. Together with the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP), NCCA holds the sole prerogative under that law to recommend to the President the 'Order of National Artists' for Filipino citizens who have contributed to building a Filipino sense of nationhood through their art forms. In Almario v. Executive Secretary (July 16 2013), the SC held the President's discretion is limited to the names submitted by NCCA and CCP -- the President cannot confer the Order on anyone not in the final list. CJP will no longer inquire nor belabor his 'wonderment' why -- despite Cecile's universal excellence in music, Lea's triumphs on the world's most prestigious stages, and Lisa's influence through ballet worldwide -- these ladies have not landed in the final list. Without begrudging any of the NAs or belittling their achievements (in fact lauding them for their much-deserved awards), CJP believes Cecile, Lea, and Lisa merit a separate category recognizing distinction that transcends national recognition. Each has long been part of NA discussions. What becomes evident is the presence of an institutional gap where recognition for globally-distinguished Filipino artists ought to stand. The President can fill this gap by creating the 'Order of Global Filipino Artists' or GFA via executive order, specifically for artists of Philippine ancestry (one or both parents Filipino at the birth of the awardee), with privileges and honors equal to or better than NAs. In time, Congress may institutionalize this category. Marcos Sr. initiated the NA Award via Proclamation No. 1001 (April 27 1972), refined by Proclamation No. 1144 (May 15 1973) and Presidential Decree No. 208 (June 7 1973). Marcos Sr. likewise issued Proclamation No. 1151 (June 7 1973), establishing the 'Award and Decoration for International Artists' for foreign talents contributing to Philippine arts/culture, premised on 'the arts and letters are universal media of expression free of the confines of geography and nationality.' In 1976/1977, pianist Van Cliburn (USA), prima ballerina Margot Fonteyn (UK), and ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev (USSR/France) were the first proclaimed; in 1982, Russian cellist/conductor Mstislav Rostropovich was recognized following his CCP performance. In this light, the notion of an 'International Artist' must be reimagined -- the current framework does not fully recognize Filipino artists who belong to a distinct class, the Filipino diaspora, whose contributions are acclaimed both within our shores and across the globe: the Global Filipino Artists. After the GFA honor is created by executive fiat and the super ladies selected as the first GFAs, the conferment should be held at Malacañan Palace, the CCP, or PICC -- 'the very institutions that have long stood as the sanctuaries of our artistic heritage.' The President may fittingly invite the three GFAs to perform and transform the conferment into a living testament to Filipino excellence before both the nation and the world. The question is no longer whether they are worthy -- they have long proven that they are. The more compelling inquiry is whether our institutional frameworks can welcome a new dimension of artistic excellence that is global in reach, yet unmistakably, indelibly Filipino in essence.
